clue.text: Maybe Victoria welcomes flag waving in tough economic circumstances

indicators.note: a flag waving moves about, so its letters are moved into a new order

explanation.surface: A patriotic picture of Victoria, the queen or the city, flying flags while the economy struggles.
explanation.walkthrough: Victoria is not the queen but the London railway terminus, which 'Maybe' marks as one example of a station.
explanation.definitionFit: Stagflation is the economists' term for stagnant growth combined with inflation, a notoriously hard combination.

clue.text: Body temperature (roughly)

parts.note: or so means roughly, approximately

explanation.surface: A rough reading of body temperature.
explanation.definitionFit: The torso is the trunk of the human body, without head or limbs.

clue.text: Feeding Reagan a cheesy, creamy mixture from France

indicators.note: the answer is feeding within these words, hidden inside them

explanation.surface: Someone serves a former US president a cheesy French dish.
explanation.definitionFit: Ganache is a French confection of chocolate and cream used to fill or ice cakes.

clue.text: Valet unveiled shiner

parts.note: a shiner is slang for a black eye

explanation.surface: A manservant reveals a bruised eye.
explanation.definitionFit: A lackey is a servant, especially a liveried footman, or a servile follower.

clue.text: Alfred reporting live court action?

indicators.note: reporting means spoken aloud, as a commentator would

parts.note: court action is tennis and live is on, as a broadcast is, giving 'tennis on'

explanation.surface: Someone reporting live from a court case.
explanation.walkthrough: The court sounds legal, but it is a tennis court; Alfred, Lord Tennyson was the Victorian Poet Laureate.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred Tennyson was the English poet, so his first name points to the surname.

clue.text: Greek character's poetic appeal before president leaves America for Italy

definitions.note: the 's stands for is, joining definition and wordplay

indicators.note: before puts the cry ahead of the rest

parts.note: O is the poetic cry of address, as in 'O Romeo'

indicators.note: leaves says the America letter departs from the president's name
for says the Italy letter is put in its place, exchanged for it

parts.note: Emmanuel Macron is the president of France
I is the international vehicle code for Italy

explanation.surface: A Greek figure's lyrical plea, made before a president quits the US for Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: MACRON, with A replaced by I, becomes MICRON.
explanation.definitionFit: Omicron is the fifteenth letter of the Greek alphabet, so a character of that script.

clue.text: Soldier: "clean bottled my piano exam"

indicators.note: bottled is British slang for drunk, so the letters stagger into a new order

parts.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like 'my!'
P is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly
an oral is a spoken exam

explanation.surface: A soldier boasts, 'I aced my piano exam'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bottled' turns CLEAN into LANCE. Cor, like 'my!', is a British cry of surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: A lance corporal is the lowest rank of non-commissioned officer in the British Army.

clue.text: Might one make hay holding some playing cards?

parts.note: a holding is a piece of farmed land, a farm
a hand is the set of cards a player holds

explanation.surface: A card player asks if holding some cards means making hay.
explanation.walkthrough: Making hay suggests profiting in a card game, but read literally a farm worker does make hay.
explanation.definitionFit: A farmhand is a labourer on a farm, whose jobs include cutting and baling hay.

clue.text: Daughter, upper-class, introduced to New Orleans gent who fills in at work

parts.note: D is the genealogical abbreviation for daughter

indicators.note: introduced to means put among, so the letter goes inside the shuffled letters
new means made afresh, so these letters are put into a new order

parts.note: U is the traditional British label for upper-class usage

explanation.surface: A posh daughter meets a gentleman from New Orleans who covers for others at work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' rearranges ORLEANS GENT, and 'introduced to' puts U within it. Filling in sounds like covering a shift; it is filling teeth.
explanation.definitionFit: A dental surgeon fills cavities in teeth as part of the daily job, a pun on standing in.

clue.text: Ms Batty, being retired, put away soft pinny

indicators.note: the soft letter is put away, tucked inside the reversed name
retired here means drawn back, so the name is read in the reverse direction

parts.note: Nora Batty is the stocking-wrinkled character in the British sitcom Last of the Summer Wine
P is piano, the musical abbreviation for soft

explanation.surface: Nora Batty, now retired, hangs up her pinafore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being retired' turns NORA into ARON, and 'put away' tucks P inside it after the first A. Nora Batty is a famously aproned figure from a long-running British TV comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: A pinny, short for pinafore, is the British informal word for an apron worn over clothes.

clue.text: One running for office against Frank rejected information JFK provided

indicators.note: against here means next to, so the two pieces sit side by side

parts.note: frank and candid both mean open and honest

indicators.note: rejected means sent back, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: ETA, estimated time of arrival, is information an airport such as New York's JFK provides

explanation.surface: A political hopeful faces an honest rival who dismissed facts supplied by President Kennedy.
explanation.walkthrough: JFK is not the president but the New York airport, whose boards give ETAs; 'rejected' makes that ATE.
explanation.definitionFit: A candidate is a person standing in an election, seeking to win a post.

clue.text: Hector is shivering in the grip of cold turkey, drained, irritable

indicators.note: held in the grip of means placed inside the surrounding letters

parts.note: C is the standard abbreviation for cold, as on a tap

indicators.note: drained means emptied of its contents, leaving just the first and last letters

parts.note: only the outside letters of turkey remain once it is emptied

indicators.note: shivering means shaking, so the name's letters are shaken into a new order

explanation.surface: Hector, shaking with withdrawal symptoms while quitting drugs, is exhausted and bad-tempered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shivering' turns HECTOR into ROTCHE, which goes 'in the grip of' C plus TY, the drained turkey.
explanation.definitionFit: Crotchety is an informal word for grumpy and easily annoyed, often of the elderly.

clue.text: Turn back the clock and relax

indicators.note: turning back means reversing the order, so the letters of the word are read backwards

parts.note: a timer is a clock that measures elapsed time

explanation.surface: Set the clocks back an hour and unwind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn back the clock' reads as a phrase about time, but the clock is a TIMER and it is the word that turns back.
explanation.definitionFit: To remit is an older sense meaning to slacken or ease off, as a fever or effort does.

clue.text: Reprimand Rover (dog)?

parts.note: Rover is a British make of car
a dog is a typical household pet

explanation.surface: Scold Rover, the family dog, which looks the classic dog's name.
explanation.walkthrough: Rover is a classic dog's name, but here it is the British car maker; the dog is the PET.
explanation.definitionFit: To carpet someone is British informal for to call them in and tell them off, as on the boss's carpet.

clue.text: King feeling sick, stabbed at the front fencing

parts.note: R is rex, Latin for king
ailing means unwell

indicators.note: the front of stabbed is its first letter

parts.note: first letter of stabbed

explanation.surface: A sick king is stabbed while fencing.
explanation.walkthrough: Fencing with stabbing suggests swordplay; here it is the barrier.
explanation.definitionFit: Railings form a fence of upright bars, so fencing in the sense of an enclosure.

clue.text: Kate's sweet William planted in west-facing ornamental lawn rockery?

indicators.note: west-facing says the hidden letters are read backwards
planted in says the answer is buried inside the following words, like a bulb in soil

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A gardening scene: Kate's sweet william flowers set into a decorative lawn and rockery.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft folded 'planted' into the definition, leaving the hidden word without an indicator; 'planted in' is that indicator. Sweet william is a flower, but here it is Prince William, Duke of Cornwall, Kate's husband.
explanation.definitionFit: The Duchy of Cornwall is the title held by the heir to the throne, so the county names William's dukedom.

clue.text: Digger's employer's mild brews left outside

indicators.note: outside says the word for left goes around the shuffled letters

parts.note: gone means left, departed

indicators.note: brews means stirs up, so the letters are mixed into a new order

explanation.surface: A miner's boss brews mild beer and has left.
explanation.walkthrough: Mild is a British style of beer, which makes 'brews' read naturally; here it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A gold mine employs miners who dig for ore, so it is a digger's workplace.

clue.text: Item released from cloud storage that might make a bit of a splash

definitions.text: Item released from cloud storage that might make a bit of a splash

parts.words: Item released from cloud storage that might make a bit of a splash
parts.note: cloud storage sounds like computing, but it is a real rain cloud letting go a single drop of water that splashes

explanation.walkthrough: Cloud storage points to online computer files; read literally, a cloud stores water and releases it a drop at a time.
explanation.definitionFit: A single drop of rain falls from a cloud and makes a small splash where it lands.

clue.text: Police search of garden wasted time

explanation.definitionFit: A dragnet is a wide, systematic police sweep for suspects, named from a fishing net.

clue.text: Blasé about leaving Beaujolais nouveau, which could raise the spirits

indicators.note: about says the letters of blasé are found mixed about in the wine's name
leaving says those letters depart from the wine's name

the letters of blasé are those to be taken out

explanation.surface: Someone is unimpressed by the new Beaujolais, a wine meant to cheer you up.
explanation.walkthrough: Take B, L, A, S, E out of BEAUJOLAIS to leave AUJOI, and 'nouveau' rearranges those. Raising the spirits sounds like lifting a mood; here it means summoning ghosts.

clue.text: High-ranking Venetian attending party beginning to get vicious
